theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What are the main aims of first aid?
options: Save life, stop it getting worse, help recovery
Find out who caused the accident and report them
Give the right medicines until the person is better
Move the person home as quickly as possible

questions.stem: You find a casualty (an injured or ill person) on the salon floor. What do you do first?
options: Roll the person over to check for injuries
Run outside to look for a doctor
Check for any danger to you and to them
Give the person a drink of water

questions.stem: After a fall, two casualties lie on the floor. One is shouting for help; the other is silent. Whom should you check first?
options: The one shouting, as she is in most pain
The silent one, who may not be breathing
Whichever one is closest to the door
The older one, whatever their condition

questions.stem: In Jamaica, which emergency numbers should you know?
options: 119 for fire and ambulance; 110 for police
110 for police only; 119 for ambulance only
119 for fire only; 110 for police and ambulance
110 for fire and ambulance; 119 for police

questions.stem: How do you open the airway of an unresponsive casualty lying on their back?
options: Tilt the head back and lift the chin
Push the chin down onto the chest
Turn the head to one side and hold it
Put a pillow under the head and neck

questions.stem: How long should you take to check for normal breathing?
options: At least one full minute
No more than 10 seconds
About 30 seconds
Until help arrives

questions.stem: An unresponsive casualty is making only slow, noisy gasps. What should you do?
options: Treat it as normal breathing and just wait
Put the casualty in the recovery position
Give sips of water to help the breathing
Call for help and start CPR straight away

questions.stem: Where do you place your hands for chest compressions on an adult?
options: On the left side of the chest, over the ribs
On the stomach, just below the bottom ribs
Heel of the hand in the centre of the chest
At the top of the chest, close to the neck

questions.stem: At about what rate should chest compressions be given?
options: About 60–80 a minute
About 100–120 a minute
About 150–180 a minute
About 30–40 a minute

questions.stem: About how deep should chest compressions be on an adult?
options: About 5–6 cm
About 1–2 cm
About 10–12 cm
As deep as you can push

questions.stem: If you are trained and willing to give rescue breaths, what is the usual ratio for an adult?
options: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath
50 compressions to 5 breaths
30 compressions to 2 breaths

questions.stem: Why should you wear disposable gloves when dealing with blood?
options: To keep your hands warm while you work
So that the casualty cannot see the wound
To protect you both from infection
So that the bandage sticks better

questions.stem: If you cannot, or will not, give rescue breaths, what should you do?
options: Wait for the ambulance without doing anything
Give breaths only, with no compressions
Give chest compressions non-stop until help
Give compressions for 1 minute, then stop

questions.stem: What does an AED (defibrillator) do?
options: Checks the heart and shocks it if needed
Gives the casualty oxygen through a mask
Pumps the chest for you so you can rest
Measures blood sugar for a diabetic

questions.stem: When the AED says it is analysing or about to give a shock, what must everyone do?
options: Keep pressing on the chest as normal
Hold the casualty's hand to calm them
Pour water on the pads to help them work
Stand clear and not touch the casualty

questions.stem: When can you stop CPR?
options: After about two minutes, if nothing has changed
When help takes over, or they breathe normally
As soon as the casualty's lips turn blue
When a bystander says it is not working

questions.stem: When should you put a casualty in the recovery position?
options: When they are awake and talking to you
When they are not breathing at all
When they have a painful broken leg
If unresponsive but breathing normally

questions.stem: Why does the recovery position help an unresponsive casualty who is breathing?
options: It keeps the airway clear and lets vomit drain
It makes the heart beat faster and much stronger
It stops any bleeding from the legs and arms
It helps the casualty wake up more quickly

questions.stem: Which item should NOT be kept in a workplace first-aid kit?
options: Sterile dressings
Disposable gloves
Painkiller tablets
A foil survival blanket

questions.stem: A client is choking but can still cough and speak. What should you do?
options: Give 5 hard back blows at once
Encourage her to keep coughing
Give her water to wash it down
Put your fingers in her mouth

questions.stem: A choking adult cannot cough, speak or breathe. What should you do first?
options: Give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades
Give her a large glass of water to drink at once
Lay her down flat on the floor and raise both legs up
Wait to see whether it clears by itself in time

questions.stem: Back blows have not cleared the blockage. What should you do next?
options: Give her more water to drink
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts
Lay her down and wait for help
Hold her upside down by the legs

questions.stem: The choking casualty becomes unresponsive. What should you do?
options: Keep giving back blows while she lies there
Sit her up and give her a drink
Put her in the recovery position and leave
Call 110 if not done, and start CPR

questions.stem: How do you control severe bleeding from a wound on the arm?
options: Wash the wound under the tap for 10 minutes
Put cotton wool straight into the wound
Press hard on the wound with a clean pad
Leave it to bleed so that it cleans itself

questions.stem: Blood soaks through the first pad. What should you do?
options: Take the pad off to look at the wound again
Put a second pad on top and keep pressing
Stop pressing so the blood can flow
Wash the pad and put it back on

questions.stem: A piece of glass is stuck in a wound. What should you do?
options: Pull it out quickly, then press on the wound
Push it further in so it stops the bleeding
Wash it out with plenty of soapy water
Leave it in and press on either side of it

questions.stem: Before you help a conscious casualty, what should you do?
options: Tell them who you are and ask if you may help
Ask them to pay for the first-aid kit you will use
Start straight away without saying anything
Wait until a family member arrives to agree

questions.stem: Which signs may show that a casualty is in shock?
options: Red, hot, dry skin and a slow pulse
Bright pink cheeks and a happy, calm mood
Pale, cold, clammy skin and a fast pulse
Itchy eyes and a runny nose

questions.stem: How should you help a casualty in shock?
options: Give a large drink of water and some food
Walk them around to keep the blood moving
Sit them up in a cold room to cool down
Lay them down, keep them warm, call 110

questions.stem: A client has a burn from hot wax. What is the first treatment?
options: Put ice cubes straight onto the burn
Cool running water for about 20 minutes
Rub butter or cooking oil into the burn
Burst any blisters so that they dry out

questions.stem: Which should you NOT do to a burn?
options: Cool it under cool running water
Take off rings near it before it swells
Put butter, toothpaste or ice on it
Cover it loosely with cling film

questions.stem: After a burn has been cooled, how should it be covered?
options: Loosely, with cling film or a clean dressing
Tightly, with a sticky plaster over the blister
With cotton wool pressed firmly onto it
With a thick layer of cream or ointment

questions.stem: A chemical has splashed into a client's eye. What should you do?
options: Rub the eye to get the chemical out
Close the eye and cover it with a pad
Put some eye drops in and carry on the service
Rinse it with lots of clean running water

questions.stem: A client feels faint while sitting in the salon chair. What should you do?
options: Give her a strong coffee to wake her up
Walk her outside quickly for fresh air
Help her to lie down and raise her legs
Leave her to sleep it off in the chair

questions.stem: During a seizure (fit), what should you do?
options: Hold the person down firmly to stop the jerking
Protect them from injury; cushion the head
Put something between the teeth
Pour cold water on the face

questions.stem: After an incident, what should be written in the accident or incident record?
options: Date, time, what happened and what was done
Only the casualty's name and their phone number
Only the cost of the first-aid items used
Who was to blame and what they should pay

questions.stem: A client has an asthma attack. How should you help?
options: Lay her flat on her back on the floor
Give her a hot drink and ask her to talk
Sit her up and help her use her inhaler
Take her inhaler away so she breathes alone

questions.stem: A client's face and lips swell after a product is used, and she struggles to breathe. What should you do?
options: Give her a cold drink and wait to see
Put more of the product on to test it
Lay her flat and leave her alone to rest quietly
Call 110; help her use her auto-injector

questions.stem: Which signs suggest a heart attack?
options: Crushing chest pain, perhaps into the arm
A rash of small, red, itchy spots on both legs
Itchy eyes and sneezing in the morning
A sore throat and a slight cough

questions.stem: A client's face drops on one side and her speech is slurred. What should you do?
options: Give her a large glass of water to drink
Suspect a stroke and call 110 at once
Let her sleep for an hour, then check her
Drive her home so she can rest in bed

questions.stem: A client with diabetes becomes shaky, sweaty and confused, but she can swallow. What should you do?
options: Give her an injection of her insulin
Give her a glass of plain water
Give her a sugary drink or sweets
Give her nothing and let her sleep

questions.stem: Which first aid should a first aider give?
options: Only what a certified course trained them in
Any treatment they have seen on a television show
Whatever a bystander tells them to do
Medicines from their own handbag

questions.stem: A client has had an electric shock from a faulty hair dryer and is still touching it. What do you do first?
options: Pull her away from it with your bare hands
Throw a bucket of water over her to cool her down
Start CPR while she is still touching it
Switch off at the mains before touching her

questions.stem: How should you help a casualty with a suspected broken arm?
options: Pull the arm straight to put the bone back
Support it as found and get medical help
Ask her to move it to see if it hurts
Rub the arm hard to ease the pain

questions.stem: A client has fallen and may have hurt her neck or back. What should you do?
options: Help her stand up and try to walk it off
Sit her up straight in a chair
Keep her still, steady her head; call 110
Roll her over onto her front to check her back

What do the letters AED stand for?
A person with known epilepsy is having a seizure. If it has not stopped, after about how many minutes should you call 110?
For about how many minutes should you pinch the soft part of the nose to stop a nosebleed?
In DRSABC, what does the letter S stand for?
In the FAST check for a stroke, what does the letter A stand for?
What is the name of a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction?
Which bandage, made from a large triangle of cloth, is used to make an arm sling?
What is it called when the heart suddenly stops pumping blood around the body?
What is the name of the flat bone in the middle of the chest that you press on during CPR?
What is the name of the serious condition in which the body overheats and cannot cool itself down?
What is the medical name for low blood sugar?
What is the name of the life-size practice doll used to learn CPR?
What is the name of the device placed over the casualty's face so that rescue breaths can be given without mouth-to-mouth contact?
What is the name of the full check of the casualty for other injuries, done after the life-saving checks?

essays.stem: Describe the primary survey (DRSABC) you would carry out on a client who collapses in the salon.
essays.modelAnswer: D is for Danger: I check that the area is safe for me, other people and the casualty, for example from spilled water, chemicals or a faulty appliance, and I make it safe. R is for Response: I kneel beside the client, tap her shoulders and ask loudly, 'Can you hear me? Open your eyes.' S is for Send for help: I shout for a colleague and ask them to call 110 and bring the AED and the first-aid kit. A is for Airway: I turn her onto her back, tilt the head back and lift the chin to open the airway. B is for Breathing: I look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. If she is breathing normally, I put her in the recovery position and keep checking. C is for CPR and Circulation: if she is not breathing normally, I start chest compressions at once and use the AED as soon as it arrives. I check for and control any severe bleeding. I follow the methods taught on the Centre's certified first-aid course.
markingPoints: Danger: makes the area safe for self, others and the casualty
Response: taps the shoulders and speaks loudly
Send for help: calls 110 and asks for the AED
Airway: head tilt and chin lift; Breathing: checked for no more than 10 seconds
CPR if not breathing normally, or the recovery position if breathing; severe bleeding controlled

essays.stem: Describe how to give CPR to an adult who is unresponsive and not breathing normally, including how to use an AED.
essays.modelAnswer: I make sure the area is safe, check for a response, call 110 (or ask someone else to) and ask for the AED. If the casualty is not breathing normally, I kneel beside her chest. I place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, on the lower half of the breastbone, put my other hand on top and lock my fingers. With my arms straight and my shoulders over my hands, I press down about 5–6 cm, at a rate of about 100–120 a minute, and let the chest come fully back up each time. If I am trained and willing, I give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions, using a face shield; if not, I give non-stop compressions. When the AED arrives, I switch it on and follow its voice prompts, placing the pads as the pictures show. Everyone stands clear while it analyses and gives a shock. I carry on CPR as it tells me, until help takes over, the person starts breathing normally, or I am too exhausted to go on. I follow the Centre's certified first-aid course, and I practise only on a manikin.
markingPoints: Safety, response, call 110 and ask for the AED
Hands in the centre of the chest, arms straight
About 5–6 cm deep at about 100–120 a minute, letting the chest come back up
30 compressions to 2 breaths if trained and willing; otherwise non-stop compressions
AED switched on early, prompts followed, everyone clear for the shock; carries on until help takes over or normal breathing returns

essays.stem: Describe how to place a casualty in the recovery position, and explain why it is used.
essays.modelAnswer: The recovery position is used for a casualty who is unresponsive but breathing normally. It keeps the airway open, because the tongue cannot fall back and block the throat, and it lets vomit or blood drain out of the mouth instead of being breathed in. I kneel beside the casualty, who is lying on her back, and remove her glasses and anything bulky from her pockets. I place the arm nearest to me at a right angle to her body, with the elbow bent and the palm up. I bring her far arm across her chest and hold the back of her hand against her near cheek. With my other hand, I lift her far knee so that the foot is flat on the floor. Keeping her hand against her cheek, I pull on the far knee to roll her towards me onto her side. I adjust the top leg so that the hip and knee are at right angles, and tilt her head back to keep the airway open. I make sure 110 has been called, and keep checking her breathing until help arrives.
markingPoints: Used for an unresponsive casualty who is breathing normally
Why: keeps the airway open and lets vomit drain
Near arm at a right angle; far hand held against the cheek; far knee raised
Rolled towards the first aider onto the side; top leg at right angles; head tilted back
Makes sure 110 is called and keeps checking breathing until help arrives

essays.stem: Describe how to control severe bleeding from a cut on a client's hand, and how to protect yourself and others from infection.
essays.modelAnswer: I put on disposable gloves, if I can get them quickly, to protect us both from infection. I sit or lay the client down and look at the wound. I press firmly on the wound with a clean pad or sterile dressing, or ask her to press on it herself while I get one, and I keep up firm pressure. If blood soaks through, I put a second pad on top and keep pressing, rather than lifting the first one. When the bleeding is under control, I bandage the pad firmly in place, but not so tightly that the fingers go pale or cold. For severe bleeding, I call 110 and watch for signs of shock. If something is stuck in the wound, I leave it in and press around it. Afterwards, I put the used dressings and gloves in a sealed bag for clinical waste, as the Centre's rules say, clean the area with disinfectant, wash my hands well and record the incident. I follow the Centre's certified first-aid course.
markingPoints: Disposable gloves to protect against infection
Firm direct pressure with a clean pad or sterile dressing
A second pad on top if blood soaks through; bandaged firmly but not too tightly
Calls 110 for severe bleeding and watches for shock; an embedded object is left in
Safe disposal of waste, cleaning, hand washing and recording

essays.stem: Describe the first aid for a burn from hot wax or a hot styling tool, and for a chemical splash on the skin, including what not to do.
essays.modelAnswer: For a burn from hot wax or a hot tool, I stop the treatment and cool the burn at once under cool or lukewarm running water for about 20 minutes. I take off rings, watches or tight items near the burn before it swells, unless they are stuck to the skin. I do not peel off wax or anything stuck to the burn. After cooling, I cover it loosely with cling film or a clean, non-fluffy dressing. I do not put on ice, butter, oil, toothpaste or creams, and I do not burst blisters. I keep the client warm, because cooling a large area can chill her. A large or deep burn, or a burn on the face, hands or feet, needs medical help, so I call 110 or send her to hospital. For a chemical splash on the skin, I wear gloves, brush off any dry powder, take off splashed clothing and rinse with plenty of cool running water for a long time. I check the product's safety data sheet and get medical help. I record the incident.
markingPoints: Cools under cool running water for about 20 minutes
Removes rings and tight items unless stuck; does not peel off stuck wax
Covers loosely with cling film or a clean, non-fluffy dressing
No ice, butter, oil, toothpaste or creams; blisters not burst; medical help for serious burns
Chemical on skin: gloves, rinse with plenty of water, remove splashed clothing, check the data sheet, get help

essays.stem: Describe how to help an adult who is choking, from mild choking to the point where they become unresponsive.
essays.modelAnswer: If an adult is choking but can cough, speak or breathe, the blockage is mild. I encourage her to keep coughing and stay with her. If she cannot cough, speak or breathe, the blockage is severe. I stand to her side and a little behind, support her chest with one hand and lean her forward. I give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of my hand, checking after each one whether the blockage has cleared. If it has not, I give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: I stand behind her, put my arms around her, place a fist between her navel and the bottom of her breastbone, hold it with my other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards. I keep repeating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts, and call 110 if it has not cleared. If she becomes unresponsive, I lower her carefully to the floor, make sure 110 has been called, and start CPR. Anyone who has had abdominal thrusts must be seen by a doctor. Back blows and thrusts are practised only on a manikin, never on a person.
markingPoints: Mild choking: encourages coughing
Severe: leans her forward and gives up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades
Then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, inwards and upwards; repeats; calls 110
If unresponsive: lowers to the floor, makes sure 110 is called, starts CPR
A doctor's check after abdominal thrusts; practised only on a manikin

essays.stem: Describe how you would recognise and respond to a severe allergic reaction in a client during a beauty treatment.
essays.modelAnswer: A severe allergic reaction can happen within minutes of contact with a product, a food or an insect sting. I watch for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, a widespread itchy rash or hives, difficulty breathing or wheezing, a hoarse voice, feeling faint or dizzy, pale, clammy skin, and a sense that something terrible is happening. If I see these signs, I stop the treatment at once and remove any product from the skin if I can do so safely. I call 110 straight away and say that it is a severe allergic reaction. If the client has her own adrenaline auto-injector, I help her to use it, as the device instructions say, usually into the outer thigh. If she is having trouble breathing, I let her sit up in the position she finds easiest; if she feels faint, I lay her down with her legs raised. I stay with her, watch her breathing and get ready to start CPR if she stops breathing normally. I note the time and the product used, record it and give the details to the ambulance crew.
markingPoints: Signs: swelling of the face, lips or throat; rash; difficulty breathing; feeling faint
Stops the treatment and removes the product if safe
Calls 110 at once
Helps her use her own adrenaline auto-injector, as the device instructions say
Positions her for breathing or faintness, watches her breathing, ready for CPR; records and hands over

essays.stem: Explain what shock is, the signs to look for, and how you would help a casualty in shock.
essays.modelAnswer: Shock is a life-threatening condition in which not enough blood and oxygen reach the body's organs. It can follow severe bleeding, serious burns, a severe allergic reaction or a heart attack. The signs include pale, cold, clammy skin, a fast, weak pulse, fast, shallow breathing, feeling sick or thirsty, dizziness, and confusion or anxiety. Later, the person may become unresponsive. To help, I first treat the cause if I can, for example by pressing on a bleeding wound, and I call 110. I lay the casualty down and, if she has no injury to the legs, raise her legs a little to help blood reach the vital organs. I loosen tight clothing and keep her warm with a blanket or coat, but I do not overheat her. I give her nothing to eat or drink, because she may need an operation. I reassure her, stay with her, and check her breathing and response until help arrives, ready to start CPR if needed.
markingPoints: Shock: not enough blood and oxygen reach the organs; names a cause
Signs: pale, cold, clammy skin; fast, weak pulse; fast breathing; dizziness or confusion
Treats the cause and calls 110
Lays her down, raises the legs if they are not injured, loosens clothing, keeps her warm
Nothing to eat or drink; reassures and monitors her, ready for CPR

essays.stem: Describe what you would say when you call 110, and what you would do after the casualty has been handed over to the ambulance crew.
essays.modelAnswer: When I call 110, I stay calm and speak clearly. I say which service I need, then give the exact address and how to find the salon, a phone number, what has happened, how many people are hurt, and the casualty's condition, for example whether she is responding and breathing, and any serious bleeding. I answer the operator's questions and follow their advice, and I keep the phone on speaker beside me if I am giving CPR. I send someone to meet the ambulance at the door. When the crew arrive, I tell them what happened, what I found, what I did and when, and pass on any medicines or products involved. Afterwards, I fill in the accident or incident record: the date, time, place, what happened, the injuries, the first aid given and by whom. I tell my supervisor, restock the first-aid kit, clean the area and dispose of waste as the Centre says. I talk to someone if I feel upset, because an emergency can be stressful. If the police are needed, I call 119.
markingPoints: Calls 110 and gives the address, what happened, the number of casualties and their condition
Follows the operator's advice; phone on speaker; someone meets the ambulance
Hands over clearly to the crew: what happened, what was found and done, and when
Fills in the accident or incident record and tells the supervisor
Restocks the kit, cleans up and disposes of waste safely, and looks after own wellbeing

essays.stem: Compare the first aid for a client who has a seizure with the first aid for a client who may be having a stroke.
essays.modelAnswer: In a seizure, the person may suddenly fall, go stiff and then jerk, may not know what is happening, and may wet herself. I keep calm, note the time and move away anything that could hurt her. I cushion her head and loosen tight clothing. I do not hold her down or put anything in her mouth. When the jerking stops, I check her breathing, put her in the recovery position and stay with her as she recovers. I call 110 if it is her first seizure, if it lasts more than 5 minutes, if she is injured, or if she does not wake up properly. In a stroke, the blood supply to part of the brain is blocked, or there is bleeding in the brain. I use the FAST check: Face drooping on one side, Arm weakness, Speech slurred, Time to call 110. A stroke always needs 110 at once. I keep her comfortable and reassured, give her nothing by mouth, note when the signs started and watch her breathing. Both need calm care and careful watching, but a stroke is always an emergency, while some seizures settle by themselves.
markingPoints: Seizure: protects from injury, cushions the head, does not hold down or put anything in the mouth
Seizure: times it; recovery position afterwards; calls 110 if first, over 5 minutes, injured or not recovering
Stroke: the FAST check (face, arm, speech, time)
Stroke: calls 110 at once, notes when the signs started, nothing by mouth, monitors
Makes a clear comparison of the two

practical1.title: CPR with an AED trainer on a manikin, and the recovery position
practical1.brief: Work as a group of 4 or 5 in the Centre's training room, following the methods taught on the Centre's certified first-aid course. Set up a scene in which a client collapses in the salon. Each member, in turn, carries out the primary survey (DRSABC) on an adult CPR manikin: checks for danger, checks for a response, sends another member to call 110 (role play only, never a real call) and fetch the AED trainer, opens the airway, and checks breathing for no more than 10 seconds. The member then gives CPR for 2 minutes, at about 100–120 compressions a minute and about 5–6 cm deep, with rescue breaths only on the manikin and through a face shield, and uses the AED trainer, following its prompts and making everyone stand clear. Another member takes over the compressions when the first one tires. All compressions, rescue breaths and AED use are on the manikin only: there are no real compressions on people. Then each member places a group partner, who agrees, in the recovery position and checks their breathing. Members take turns as first aider, caller, timekeeper and photographer. Fill in an incident record for the scene. Photograph each stage below. Hand in once for the whole group, with the incident records.
materials: Adult CPR manikins, with face shields and the manikin maker's cleaning wipes
An AED trainer with training pads (it cannot give a real shock)
A first-aid kit and disposable gloves
A timer, or a phone metronome set at about 110 beats a minute
photos: The scene set up, with the manikin, AED trainer and first-aid kit
Checking for a response and opening the airway on the manikin
The hand position for chest compressions on the manikin
The AED trainer pads on the manikin, with everyone standing clear
The change-over between two members giving compressions
A member placing a partner in the recovery position
checklist: Checked for danger and for a response before touching the casualty
Sent for help clearly: 110 and the AED (role play)
Opened the airway with a head tilt and chin lift, and checked breathing for no more than 10 seconds
Placed the hands correctly in the centre of the chest, with the arms straight
Gave compressions at about 100–120 a minute and about 5–6 cm deep, letting the chest come back up
Used the AED trainer safely, following its prompts and keeping everyone clear
Placed a partner in the recovery position correctly and checked their breathing
safety: Never give chest compressions, rescue breaths or AED pads to a real person: use the manikin only
Clean the manikin's face and use a fresh face shield between members, as the manikin maker says
Do not make real calls to 110 during the practice
Kneel on a mat and take turns, so that no one strains their back or knees
Handle partners gently in the recovery position, and stop if anyone feels pain
Follow the Centre's certified first-aid course and the assessor's instructions

practical2.title: Salon first-aid scenarios: bleeding, a burn, choking, a sling and an incident report
practical2.brief: Work as a group of 4 or 5, following the methods taught on the Centre's certified first-aid course. The assessor sets up four salon scenario stations. Every member takes the first-aider role at each station, while the others take turns as the casualty, the helper and the photographer. Station 1: a deep cut to the hand from scissors (no real wound: a make-up mark or a training wound is used). Put on gloves, press on the 'wound' with a pad, add a second pad, and bandage it firmly but not tightly. Station 2: a burn on the forearm from hot wax. Show cooling under cool running water (time it for a short while for the assessor, then explain the full 20 minutes), remove any ring or watch, and cover it loosely with cling film. Station 3: an adult who is choking. Show back blows and abdominal thrusts on a choking manikin or training vest only, never on a person, and explain what to do if the casualty becomes unresponsive. Station 4: a suspected broken arm. Support the arm in a sling made from a triangular bandage, on a partner who agrees. Then each member fills in one incident record for a station and role-plays the 110 call, giving the right details. Photograph each stage below. Hand in once for the whole group, with the incident records.
materials: A first-aid kit: sterile dressings, pads, bandages, triangular bandages, cling film, tape, scissors and disposable gloves
Training wounds or make-up to mark a 'wound' (no real cuts)
A sink with cool running water, or a bowl and jug, and towels
A choking manikin or a choking training vest
A bag for used dressings and gloves, as the Centre's rules say

The 110 call role play, with the member's notes
checklist: Checked for danger, said who they were and asked consent before helping
Wore gloves, pressed firmly with a pad, added a second pad when needed, and bandaged correctly
Cooled the burn with cool running water, explained the 20 minutes, removed jewellery, covered with cling film, and named things not to use
Showed back blows and abdominal thrusts correctly on the manikin or vest only, and said what to do if the casualty becomes unresponsive
Supported the arm in a well-fitted sling and checked that the fingers stayed pink and warm
Gave the right details in the 110 call role play
Filled in a clear incident record
Disposed of used dressings and gloves safely and washed their hands
safety: No real wounds: use make-up or training wounds only
Never give back blows or abdominal thrusts to a person: use the choking manikin or vest only
Do not make real calls to 110 during the practice
Tie slings and bandages firmly but not tightly; check that the fingers stay pink and warm
Keep the floor dry around the water station
Follow the Centre's certified first-aid course and the assessor's instructions
